lessons.title: Alkyd, Polyurethane, and Epoxy Resin Systems
lessons.body:
Alkyd resins are the workhorse of solvent-based paints in Africa. They are made by reacting vegetable oils like soya or linseed with acids and alcohols. For a basic alkyd, you need a reaction kettle with a thermometer, stirrer, and condenser. Start by heating 100 kg of soya oil to 240Â°C, then add 50 kg of pentaerythritol and 70 kg of phthalic anhydride. Hold at 240Â°C for 3 hours until the acid value drops below 10 mg KOH/g. Cool to 180Â°C and thin with 50 kg of mineral spirits. This gives a medium-oil alkyd for brushable enamel.

Polyurethane resins come in two parts: a polyol and an isocyanate. For a moisture-cure polyurethane, you mix a polyol with toluene diisocyanate (TDI) at 60Â°C for 2 hours. The ratio is critical: 1 mole of polyol to 2 moles of TDI. Use a nitrogen blanket to prevent moisture from reacting. Polyurethane gives tough, chemical-resistant coatings for floors and metal. In Africa, it's popular for concrete floors in factories because it withstands heavy foot traffic and cleaning chemicals.

Epoxy resins are also two-part: resin and hardener. The most common is bisphenol A diglycidyl ether (BADGE) with a polyamine hardener. Mix 100 parts resin with 50 parts hardener by weight. Epoxy cures at room temperature but can be accelerated to 60Â°C for faster set. It has excellent adhesion to metal and concrete, making it ideal for water tanks and boat hulls. However, epoxy is not UV stableâit yellows and chalks in sunlight, so use it only indoors or topcoat with polyurethane.

In your workshop, always check resin quality: alkyd should be clear and free of gel particles; polyurethane should not have a skin; epoxy should be uniform. Store resins in sealed drums away from moisture. When scaling up, keep records of temperature, time, and acid value. A simple acid-base titration kit costs about $50 and is essential for alkyd production.

lessons.title: Solvent Selection and Blending
lessons.body:
Solvents dissolve the resin and control drying. The key properties are evaporation rate, solvency power, and cost. In Africa, common solvents are mineral spirits (white spirit), xylene, toluene, acetone, and butyl acetate. Mineral spirits are cheap and slow-evaporating, good for brush application. Xylene and toluene are faster and stronger but more toxic and flammable. Acetone is very fast but weak for alkyds. Butyl acetate is a medium evaporator for polyurethanes.

Use the 'solubility parameter' concept without complex math: if the resin and solvent have similar polarity, they mix. Alkyds are non-polar, so use mineral spirits or xylene. Polyurethanes need esters like butyl acetate. Epoxies often use ketones like methyl ethyl ketone (MEK) or acetone. A simple test: put 10 g of resin in a jar, add 20 ml of solvent, stir, and see if it dissolves clear. If cloudy, try another solvent.

Blending solvents gives better control. For a brushable enamel, blend 70% mineral spirits with 30% xylene. This gives a drying time of 4-6 hours. For spray application, use 50% xylene, 30% toluene, 20% butyl acetate for a 30-minute flash-off. Always blend by volume in a clean drum with a stirrer. Never mix solvents in a plastic containerâuse metal or glass. Measure with a graduated cylinder or flow meter.

Safety and cost: xylene and toluene are hazardous; use gloves and respirator. In many African countries, mineral spirits cost $2-3 per liter, xylene $3-4, butyl acetate $5-6. Buy in 200-liter drums to save 30%. Store solvents in a cool, ventilated shed away from sparks. Test each batch for evaporation rate by putting 10 ml in a dish and timing how long to dry. Record results. A good blend will give a smooth film without orange peel or blushing.

lessons.title: Formulation of Enamels and Varnishes
lessons.body:
Enamel is a pigmented solvent-based paint that dries to a hard, glossy film. A basic white enamel formula for 100 kg: 40 kg alkyd resin (60% solids), 25 kg titanium dioxide, 20 kg mineral spirits, 10 kg xylene, 3 kg calcium carbonate (filler), 1 kg driers (cobalt and zirconium), and 1 kg anti-skinning agent. Mix in a high-speed disperser: first add resin and solvents, then slowly add pigments. Disperse for 30 minutes at 1500 rpm. Then add driers and anti-skin. Check viscosity with a Ford cup #4âshould be 60-80 seconds. If too thick, add solvent; if too thin, add more resin.

Varnish is a clear coating without pigment. For a polyurethane varnish, mix 50 kg polyurethane resin (50% solids), 30 kg butyl acetate, 15 kg xylene, 3 kg UV absorber, and 2 kg flow agent. Stir gently to avoid bubbles. Varnish is used on wood to show grain. In Africa, it's popular for furniture and doors. Apply with brush or spray. Drying time is 2-4 hours for touch, 24 hours for full cure.

For epoxy enamel, use 50 kg epoxy resin, 20 kg titanium dioxide, 20 kg xylene, 5 kg butyl acetate, and 5 kg hardener (added just before use). Pot life is 4-6 hours at 25Â°C. Mix only what you can use in that time. Epoxy enamel is excellent for metal railings and machinery.

Quality checks: test adhesion with cross-hatch tape test; test gloss with a gloss meter (60Â° reading should be >80 for enamel); test hardness with a pencil (2H or harder). Store enamels in lined cans to prevent reaction with metal. Label with batch number and date. In a small African workshop, you can produce 200 liters per day with a 500-liter disperser and a few drums.

lessons.title: Reaction Kettles and Process Control
lessons.body:
A reaction kettle is a heated vessel with a stirrer, thermometer, condenser, and nitrogen inlet. For alkyd production, you need a stainless steel kettle of at least 500 liters. In Africa, many small factories use mild steel kettles with a glass-lined interior to resist acids. The kettle sits on a gas or electric heater. A simple setup costs $5,000-$10,000. You also need a condenser to recover solvents and a receiver flask.

Process control means monitoring temperature, time, and acid value. For alkyd, charge oil and polyol, heat to 240Â°C with stirring at 200 rpm. Hold for 1 hour. Then add acid and heat to 240Â°C again. Take a sample every 30 minutes: dissolve 1 g resin in 20 ml ethanol, add 2 drops phenolphthalein, and titrate with 0.1N KOH until pink. Acid value = (ml KOH Ã 5.6)/g sample. Stop when acid value is below 10. Cool to 180Â°C, add solvent, and stir for 30 minutes.

For polyurethane, control is simpler: mix polyol and isocyanate at 60Â°C for 2 hours under nitrogen. Check NCO content by titration: react with dibutylamine, then titrate with HCl. NCO% should be 3-5%. For epoxy, mix resin and hardener at room temperature; no heating needed. But control the mix ratio preciselyâuse a digital scale.

Safety in the kettle area: never leave a hot kettle unattended. Keep a fire extinguisher (CO2 or dry powder) nearby. Use a fume hood or exhaust fan. In Africa, power cuts are commonâhave a backup generator for the stirrer and heater. Clean the kettle after each batch with solvent and scrape. Record all data in a logbook: batch number, temperatures, times, acid values, and yields. This helps you repeat good batches and troubleshoot bad ones.

lessons.title: Safety Measures for Solvent Handling
lessons.body:
Solvents are flammable and toxic. In Africa, many workshops lack proper ventilation, so safety is critical. Always store solvents in a cool, dry, locked shed away from sunlight and ignition sources. Use metal drums with tight bungs. Keep only one day's supply in the work area. Never smoke or use open flames near solvents. Vapors can travel 10 meters and ignite. Use explosion-proof electrical fittings if possible; otherwise, keep motors and switches outside the solvent zone.

Personal protective equipment (PPE): wear nitrile gloves (not latexâsolvents pass through latex), safety goggles, and a respirator with organic vapor cartridges. A half-mask respirator costs $30-$50 and cartridges last 40 hours. Wear cotton overalls, not synthetic, because synthetics can generate static sparks. Have a eyewash station and a safety shower nearby. If solvent splashes in eyes, rinse for 15 minutes with clean water.

Ventilation: use a fan to push air from the work area to outside. A simple exhaust fan of 0.5 kW can move 3000 mÂ³/hour. Open windows and doors. Never work in a closed room. If you feel dizzy, headache, or nausea, leave immediately and get fresh air. Solvent poisoning can cause liver and kidney damage over time.

Fire safety: keep a CO2 or dry powder extinguisher (5 kg) at each exit. Never use water on solvent firesâit spreads them. Train everyone to use the extinguisher: pull pin, aim at base, squeeze, sweep. Have a fire blanket. In case of spill, absorb with sand or sawdust, then sweep into a metal container. Do not wash down drains. Dispose of solvent waste through a licensed handler. In many African cities, you can contact local environmental authorities for disposal. Keep a first aid kit and a list of emergency numbers.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Solvent-Based Paint Issues
lessons.body:
Common problems in solvent-based paints include slow drying, orange peel, blushing, sagging, and poor adhesion. Slow drying: usually caused by too much slow solvent (mineral spirits) or insufficient driers. Fix by adding 0.1% cobalt drier or replacing 10% of solvent with xylene. In humid African coastal areas, blushing (white haze) occurs when moisture condenses in the film. Prevent by adding 2% butyl cellosolve or drying in a warm room above 25Â°C.

Orange peel (bumpy surface) happens when solvent evaporates too fast or spray gun is too far. Use a slower solvent blend (more mineral spirits) and spray at 20-25 cm distance with 40 psi pressure. For brush marks, thin the paint by 5% with xylene and brush in one direction. Sagging (runs) means too much paint or too thin. Apply thinner coats, wait 10 minutes between coats. If sagging occurs, sand and recoat.

Poor adhesion: often due to oily or dirty substrate. Clean metal with acetone or xylene, then sand with 120-grit. For concrete, etch with 10% muriatic acid, rinse, and dry. If paint peels, check for moisture in the substrateâuse a moisture meter (should be <5%). For epoxy on metal, prime with a wash primer first. In Africa, dust is a problemâpaint in a clean area or use a tack cloth.

Other issues: skinning in the can (add 0.2% anti-skin), settling of pigments (add 0.5% anti-settling agent like fumed silica), and yellowing of alkyds in dark (use UV absorber). Keep a troubleshooting log: record problem, cause, and fix. Test small batches before full production. A simple test panel: apply paint on a 10x10 cm metal plate, dry, then scratch with a coin. If it flakes, adhesion is poor. Adjust formula and retest.

quiz.q: What is the typical reaction temperature for making a medium-oil alkyd resin?
quiz.explanation: Alkyd resins are typically processed at 240Â°C to achieve the correct acid value and viscosity.

quiz.q: Which solvent is most suitable for dissolving a polyurethane resin?
quiz.explanation: Polyurethanes require ester solvents like butyl acetate for proper solvency.

quiz.q: What is the function of a condenser in a reaction kettle?
options: B) To recover solvents and prevent loss
quiz.explanation: The condenser cools vapors back to liquid, recovering solvent and preventing escape.

quiz.q: Which PPE is essential when handling xylene?
quiz.explanation: Nitrile gloves resist solvents; latex gloves allow solvents to pass through.

quiz.q: What is the acid value target for a finished alkyd resin?
quiz.explanation: A low acid value (below 10) indicates complete reaction and good resin quality.

quiz.q: Which test measures the drying time of a solvent-based paint?
quiz.explanation: Touch dry time is a simple test where you touch the film to see when it no longer sticks.

quiz.q: What causes blushing in solvent-based paints?
options: B) Moisture condensation in the film
quiz.explanation: Blushing occurs when moisture from humid air condenses into the drying film, causing a white haze.

quiz.q: Which solvent blend is recommended for spray application of enamel?
quiz.explanation: This blend provides fast evaporation and good solvency for spray application.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an anti-skinning agent in enamel?
options: B) To prevent a skin from forming in the can
quiz.explanation: Anti-skinning agents like methyl ethyl ketoxime prevent surface skinning during storage.

quiz.q: Which resin system is not UV stable and will yellow in sunlight?
quiz.explanation: Epoxy resins yellow and chalk when exposed to UV light, so they are for interior use.

quiz.q: What is the correct mix ratio for a typical two-part epoxy?
quiz.explanation: Common epoxy resin to hardener ratio is 100 parts resin to 50 parts hardener by weight.

quiz.q: How do you test for NCO content in polyurethane production?
quiz.explanation: NCO content is determined by reacting with dibutylamine and titrating with HCl.

quiz.q: What is the recommended storage for solvents?
options: B) In a cool, dry, locked shed
quiz.explanation: Solvents should be stored in a cool, dry, locked shed away from ignition sources.

quiz.q: Which fire extinguisher is safe for solvent fires?
quiz.explanation: CO2 or dry powder extinguishers are effective and safe for flammable liquid fires.

quiz.q: What is the first step in troubleshooting poor adhesion?
quiz.explanation: Poor adhesion is often due to a dirty or oily substrate, so cleaning is the first fix.

quiz.q: Which pigment is commonly used for white enamel?
quiz.explanation: Titanium dioxide provides high opacity and brightness for white paints.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a nitrogen blanket in polyurethane production?
quiz.explanation: Nitrogen displaces air and moisture, preventing unwanted reactions with isocyanate.

quiz.q: How often should you take a sample for acid value during alkyd production?
quiz.explanation: Sampling every 30 minutes allows you to monitor the reaction progress and stop at the right acid value.

quiz.q: What is a Ford cup used for?
quiz.explanation: A Ford cup measures the flow time of a liquid, which indicates viscosity.

quiz.q: Which solvent is fastest evaporating?
quiz.explanation: Acetone has a very high evaporation rate compared to the other solvents listed.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spray distance for enamel to avoid orange peel?
quiz.explanation: Spraying at 20-25 cm gives proper atomization and avoids dry, bumpy films.

quiz.q: What does a gloss meter measure?
quiz.explanation: A gloss meter measures the reflectance of a surface at a specific angle, indicating gloss level.

quiz.q: Which additive prevents pigment settling in enamel?
quiz.explanation: Fumed silica acts as a thixotropic agent, preventing pigment settling.

quiz.q: What is the pot life of a typical epoxy enamel at 25Â°C?
quiz.explanation: Epoxy enamel has a pot life of 4-6 hours before it becomes too viscous to apply.

quiz.q: Which test checks adhesion of a paint film?
quiz.explanation: The cross-hatch tape test involves cutting a grid and pulling tape to see if paint flakes off.

quiz.q: What is the main hazard of solvent vapors?
options: A) They are flammable and toxic
quiz.explanation: Solvent vapors can ignite easily and cause health problems if inhaled.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do if you spill solvent?
options: B) Absorb with sand or sawdust
D) Use a fan to dry
quiz.explanation: Absorbing with inert material like sand prevents spreading and reduces fire risk.

quiz.q: Which resin requires a hardener added just before use?
quiz.explanation: Epoxy is a two-part system where the hardener is mixed in immediately before application.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a moisture meter in painting?
quiz.explanation: A moisture meter ensures the substrate is dry enough (below 5%) to prevent peeling.

quiz.q: Which solvent is least toxic?
quiz.explanation: Mineral spirits are generally less toxic than aromatic solvents like xylene and toluene.
